parts.article:
The Fruit Book
 
It’s not every scientist who writes books for people who can’t read. And how many scientists want their books to look as dog-eared as possible? But Patricia Shanley, an ethnobotanist, wanted to give something back. After the poorest people of the Amazon allowed her to study their land and its ecology, she turned her research findings into a picture book that tells the local people how to get a good return from their trees without succumbing to the lure of a quick buck from a logging company. It has proved a big success.
 
(A) A Book for the People The book is called Fruit Trees and Useful Plants in the Lives of Amazonians, but is better known simply as the “fruit book”. The second edition was produced at the request of politicians in western Amazonia. Its blend of hard science and local knowledge on the use and trade of 35 native forest species has been so well received (and well used) that no less a dignitary than Brazil’s environment minister, Marina Silva, has written the foreword. “There is nothing else like the Shanley book,” says Adalberto Veríssimo, director of the Institute of People and the Environment of the Amazon. “It gives science back to the poor, to the people who really need it.”
 
(B) The Origin: A Plea from the Union Shanley’s work on the book began a decade ago, with a plea for help from the Rural Workers’ Union of Paragominas, a Brazilian town whose prosperity is based on exploitation of timber. The union realised that logging companies would soon be knocking on the doors of the caboclos, peasant farmers living on the Rio Capim, an Amazon tributary in the Brazilian state of Pará. Isolated and illiterate, the caboclos would have little concept of the true value of their trees; communities downstream had already sold off large blocks of forest for a pittance. “What they wanted to know was how valuable the forests were,” recalls Shanley, then a researcher in the area for the Massachusetts-based Woods Hole Research Centre.
 
(C) Timber vs. Fruit: The Economic Question The Rural Workers’ Union wanted to know whether harvesting wild fruits would make economic sense in the Rio Capim. “There was a lot of interest in trading non-timber forest products (NTFPs),” Shanley says. At the time, environmental groups and green minded businesses were promoting the idea. This was the view presented in a seminal paper, Valuation of an Amazonian Rainforest, published in Nature in 1989. The researchers had calculated that revenues from the sale of fruits could far exceed those from a one-off sale of trees to loggers. “The union was keen to discover whether it made more sense conserving the forest for subsistence use and the possible sale of fruit, game and medicinal plants, than selling trees for timber,” says Shanley. Whether it would work for the caboclos was far from clear.
 
(D) Fieldwork and Local Species Although Shanley had been invited to work in the Rio Capim, some caboclos were suspicious. “When Patricia asked if she could study my forest,” says Joao Fernando Moreira Brito, “my neighbours said she was a foreigner who’d come to rob me of my trees.” In the end, Moreira Brito, or Mangueira as he is known, welcomed Shanley and worked on her study. His land, an hour’s walk from the Rio Capim, is almost entirely covered with primary forest. A study of this and other tracts of forest selected by the communities enabled Shanley to identify three trees, found throughout the Amazon, whose fruit was much favoured by the caboclos: bacuri (Platonia insignis), uxi (Endopleura uchi) and piquia (Caryocar villosum). The caboclos used their fruits, extracted oils, and knew what sort of wildlife they attracted. But, in the face of aggressive tactics from the logging companies, they had no measure of the trees’ financial worth. The only way to find out, Shanley decided, was to start from scratch with a scientific study. “From a scientific point of view, hardly anything was known about these trees,” she says. But six years of field research yielded a mass of data on their flowering and fruiting behaviour. During 1993 and 1994, 30 families weighed everything they used from the forest – game, fruit, fibre, medicinal plants – and documented its source.
 
(E) The Impact of Logging and Fire After three logging sales and a major fire in 1997, the researchers were also able to study the ecosystem’s reaction to logging and disturbance. They carried out a similar, though less exhaustive, study in 1999, this time with 15 families. The changes were striking. Average annual household consumption of forest fruit had fallen from 89 to 28 kilograms between 1993 and 1999. “What we found,” says Shanley, “was that fruit collection could coexist with a certain amount of logging, but after the forest fire, it dropped dramatically.” Over the same period, fibre use also dropped from around 20 to 4 kilograms. The fire and logging also changed the nature of the caboclo diet. In 1993 most households ate game two or three times a month. By 1999 some were fortunate if they ate game more than two or three times a year.
 
(F) Trees and Game: The Hidden Value The loss of certain species of tree was especially significant. Shanley’s team persuaded local hunters to weigh their catch, noting the trees under which the animals were caught. Over the year, they trapped five species of game averaging 232 kilogrammes under piquia trees. Under copaiba, they caught just two species averaging 63 kilogrammes; and under uxi, four species weighing 38 kilogrammes. At last, the team was getting a handle on which trees were worth keeping, and which could reasonably be sold. “This showed that selling piquia trees to loggers for a few dollars made little sense,” explains Shanley. “Their local value lies in providing a prized fruit, as well as flowers which attract more game than any other species.”
 
(G) Reality Check: The Limits of NTFPs As a result of these studies, Shanley had to tell the Rural Workers’ Union of Paragominas that the Nature thesis could not be applied wholesale to their community – harvesting NTFPs would not always yield more than timber sales. Fruiting patterns of trees such as uxi were unpredictable, for example. In 1994, one household collected 3,654 uxi fruits; the following year, none at all.
 
(H) Subsistence vs. Commerce This is not to say that wild fruit trees were unimportant. On the contrary, argues Shanley, they are critical for subsistence, something that is often ignored in much of the current research on NTFPs, which tends to focus on their commercial potential. Geography was another factor preventing the Rio Capim caboclos from establishing a serious trade in wild fruit: villagers in remote areas could not compete with communities collecting NTFPs close to urban markets, although they could sell them to passing river boats.
 
(I) Empowering Through Education But Shanley and her colleagues decided to do more than just report their results to the union. Together with two of her research colleagues, Shanley wrote the fruit book. This, the Bible and a publication on medicinal plants co-authored by Shanley and designed for people with minimal literacy skills are about the only books you will see along this stretch of the Rio Capim. The first print run was only 3,000 copies, but the fruit book has been remarkably influential, and is used by colleges, peasant unions, industries and the caboclos themselves. Its success is largely due to the fact that people with poor literacy skills can understand much of the information it contains about the non-timber forest products, thanks to its illustrations, anecdotes, stories and songs. “The book doesn’t tell people what to do,” says Shanley, “but it does provide them with choices.” The caboclos who have used the book now have a much better understanding of which trees to sell to the loggers, and which to protect.

questions.question: A description of Shanley’s initial data collection

analyses.content: “Data collection” 对应原文的 “weighed everything... documented its source”。
(Paragraph D) “...During 1993 and 1994, 30 families weighed everything they used from the forest ... and documented its source.”
题目要求找到对Shanley最初数据收集的描述。原文D段详细描述了她“start from scratch（从零开始）”，以及“During 1993 and 1994, 30 families weighed everything... and documented its source（称重并记录来源）”，这就是数据收集过程，选 D。

questions.question: Why a government official also contributes to the book

analyses.content: 题目问为什么一位政府官员也为这本书做出了贡献。原文A段提到巴西环境部长Marina Silva因为书“so well received（如此受欢迎）”而写了“foreword（前言）”，写前言即contributes，选 A。
“Government official” 对应 “environment minister”，“contributes” 对应 “written the foreword”。
(Paragraph A) “...Brazil’s environment minister, Marina Silva, has written the foreword.”

questions.question: Reasons why the community asked Shanley to conduct the research

analyses.content: 题目问社区要求Shanley进行研究的原因。原文C段指出工会“wanted to know（想知道）”采摘野果在经济上是否合算，以及“keen to discover（渴望发现）”保护森林是否比卖木材更有意义，这是进行特定研究的动因，选 C。
虽然B段提到了“plea（请求）”，但C段具体阐述了请求背后的核心研究动机/原因（Timber vs. Fruit 的经济比较）。
(Paragraph C) “The Rural Workers’ Union wanted to know whether harvesting wild fruits would make economic sense...”

questions.question: Reference to the starting point of her research

analyses.content: (Paragraph B) “Shanley’s work on the book began a decade ago, with a plea for help...”
题目提到她研究起点的参考。原文B段开头明确说“Shanley’s work ... began a decade ago, with a plea for help（工作始于十年前的一个求助）”，这是最直接的起点，选 B。
“Starting point” 对应原文的 “began... with...”。

questions.question: Two factors that alter food consumption patterns

analyses.content: 题目提到改变食物消费模式的两个因素。原文E段标题即“The Impact of Logging and Fire”，文中提到“fire and logging also changed the nature of the caboclo diet（火灾和伐木改变了饮食本质）”，选 E。
“Two factors” 对应 “logging sales and a major fire”。
(Paragraph E) “The fire and logging also changed the nature of the caboclo diet.”
题目问为什么这本书是成功的。原文I段提到“Its success is largely due to...（其成功主要归功于……）”，并解释是因为文化水平低的人也能看懂，选 I。
直接定位关键词 “success”。
(Paragraph I) “Its success is largely due to the fact that people with poor literacy skills can understand...”

analyses.content: 题目说森林火灾导致当地村民消费更少的____。原文E段提到“consumption of forest fruit had fallen（森林水果的消费量下降了）”，填 forest fruit。
“Consume less” 对应 “consumption... had fallen”。也可填 fruit。
(Paragraph E) “Average annual household consumption of forest fruit had fallen...”
并列关系，接着找 dropped/fallen 的对象。
(Paragraph E) “Over the same period, fibre use also dropped...”
题目并列项，消费更少的还有____。原文E段接着说“fibre use also dropped（纤维使用也下降了）”，填 fibre。
题目说在____下捕获的猎物最少。原文F段列出数据：piquia下232kg，copaiba下63kg，uxi下38kg（最少），填 uxi。
比较数字大小，38kg为 least amount。
(Paragraph F) “...and under uxi, four species weighing 38 kilogrammes.”
题目说产量也是____。原文G段提到像uxi这样的树的“Fruiting patterns... were unpredictable（结果模式是不可预测的）”，填 unpredictable。
“Yield” 对应 “Fruiting patterns / collected... none at all”。
(Paragraph G) “Fruiting patterns of trees such as uxi were unpredictable...”
(Paragraph F) “This showed that selling piquia trees to loggers for a few dollars made little sense.”
题目说因此保留____是更合理的。原文F段末尾说卖掉 piquia trees 没意义（little sense），因为它们有高价值，“Worth keeping” 即 implied reasonable to keep，填 piquia trees。
题目是正向“keep”，原文是反向“selling... little sense”。
题目说除了卖给伐木工，所有的树还可以用于____。原文H段说它们对于“subsistence（生存/自给自足）”至关重要，填 subsistence。
“Used for” 对应 “critical for”。
(Paragraph H) “...they are critical for subsistence...”
题目说这一点常被忽视，因为大多数研究通常关注树木的____。原文H段说目前的研究倾向于关注它们的“commercial potential（商业潜力）”，填 commercial potential。
“Focuses on” 对应 “tends to focus on”。
(Paragraph H) “...current research on NTFPs, which tends to focus on their commercial potential.”
题目说书的目的是提供关于____的信息。原文I段提到书包含关于“non-timber forest products（非木材森林产品）”的信息，填 non-timber forest products。
缩写 NTFPs 也可以，但原文I段给出全称，填全称更稳妥。
(Paragraph I) “...understand much of the information it contains about the non-timber forest products...”
